passage:
"Why is the traffic worse since they opened the new flyover, Sarita Aunty? It was supposed to fix it."
Sarita laughed, stirring her tea. "You tell me, Yusuf. You're the one doing the project."
"Okay. The flyover made the road faster. So more people started driving instead of taking the bus."
"And?"
"So, more cars. The buses got fewer passengers, so some routes were cut. So even more people drive." He frowned. "And the flyover ends at the market signal, so everything piles up there."
"So is the flyover the problem?"
"Not by itself. It's the flyover plus the buses plus the signal plus people's choices. It's all connected."
"Put that in your project."
"I'll draw it as a loop."

qa.q: Where does the flyover end?
qa.a: At the market signal.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf frown in the middle of his explanation?
qa.a: He was puzzled, realising the problem was more tangled than he thought, with each change feeding the next.

qa.q: How could Yusuf make his project clearer?
qa.a: Draw the loop he mentions, with arrows showing how more cars, fewer buses and the signal all feed each other.

qa.q: How might a bus driver see the same situation?
qa.a: Fewer passengers and cut routes would feel like a slow loss of work, a part Yusuf sees only as one link in the chain.

grounding: It shows a teenager tracing how a flyover, buses, a signal and people's choices interact as one system.

passage: Last year Payal and I were put in charge of fixing food waste in our school canteen. I thought it was simple: tell kids to finish their plates. It didn't work. Payal said, "Ritu, let's just watch first." So we watched for a week. Kids threw food because lunch break was only twenty minutes, and the queue took ten. The canteen made big portions because the cook was paid by the plate. And the dal was always cold because the burner was shared with the tea. Everything was tied to everything else. When the principal moved lunch break to thirty minutes and the cook got a second burner, waste dropped by half. I still think about how the obvious answer was the wrong one.

qa.q: How long was the lunch break at first?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Ritu realise after watching for a week?
qa.a: That the waste came from many linked causes, like time, portion size, pay and a shared burner, not just from kids being careless.

qa.q: Why did the final changes work when "finish your plates" didn't?
qa.a: They targeted the connected causes, like time and cold food, instead of blaming students.

qa.q: How might the cook have seen the waste problem?
qa.a: The cook may have seen big portions as part of doing the job, since the cook was paid by the plate, not as a cause of waste.

grounding: It shows a teenager discovering that canteen waste came from several interacting variables in one system.

passage: Eco-club note, Alka Ma'am. Our garden's tomato plants had few fruits this term. Most students blamed the soil. Dolma, fourteen, spent two weeks watching and came back with a diagram. The gardener had sprayed the rose bed for aphids; the spray drifted onto the marigolds; fewer bees came; so the tomatoes got fewer visits too. She also noted that the new wall had cut the evening breeze, which suited the aphids. "It's not one thing," she said. "It's a web." I asked her to present it to the gardener as a question, not as blame. Next term we will try a separate spray zone and more marigolds.

qa.q: What had the gardener sprayed the rose bed for?
qa.a: Aphids.

qa.q: What does "It's not one thing, it's a web" show about how Dolma was thinking?
qa.a: She understood that the garden's parts affect each other, so one change like spraying could ripple through to the tomatoes.

qa.q: Why did Alka ask her to present it as a question, not as blame?
qa.a: So the gardener would feel part of solving it instead of defensive, which makes change more likely.

qa.q: How might the gardener feel hearing Dolma's diagram?
qa.a: Possibly surprised and a bit defensive at first, but interested if it is framed as working together.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a teenager mapping how spray, bees, wind and plants interact in the school garden.

passage: 12 Aug. Park flooded again. Yusuf says it's just too much rain. But it rained this much last year and the swings were fine. So after school we walked around it like detectives. 1) The new building next door has covered its whole plot in cement, so water can't soak in. 2) The drain near the gate is full of chip packets. 3) The gardener cut back the hedge, and now soil slides onto the path and into the drain. Any one of these alone maybe wouldn't matter. Together the water has nowhere to go, and now there are mosquitoes, so Ammi won't let my little brother out. Yusuf said I'm overthinking. Maybe. I'm going to draw arrows between all of these tonight. – Kashish

qa.q: What was blocking the drain near the gate?
qa.a: Chip packets were blocking it.

qa.q: Why does Kashish want to draw arrows tonight?
qa.a: Kashish feels curious and determined to understand the flooding, believing the causes work together, and wants to see how they connect.

qa.q: What could Kashish do next with these findings?
qa.a: Kashish could show the drawing to the colony committee or a teacher, so the adults who manage the drain and park can act.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see the problem differently?
qa.a: Yusuf sees one simple cause, heavy rain, and thinks Kashish is making it complicated.

grounding: Shows a teenager tracing how several separate causes combine to flood a park and affect the family.

passage: In their village, Pooja, fifteen, was helping her father Kamal decide what to do about the yellowing cotton. "Use more fertilizer," the shopkeeper had said. Pooja frowned. "But Papa, it's rained for two weeks. The roots might be waterlogged. More fertilizer might wash into the canal. And the neighbour's field didn't turn yellow, and he has better drains." She sketched it in her notebook: rain, drains, roots, fertilizer, canal, arrows everywhere. Kamal looked at it for a long time. "So first we fix the drain." "And ask the agriculture officer," Pooja said. "Before we spend anything." Kamal folded the page and put it in his shirt pocket.

qa.q: What had the shopkeeper told them to use?
qa.a: More fertilizer.

qa.q: What was Pooja thinking when she frowned at the shopkeeper's advice?
qa.a: She was doubtful and uneasy, sensing that the problem involved more than just fertilizer.

qa.q: Which choice made sense, and why?
qa.a: Fixing the drain and asking the agriculture officer, because it addressed the whole system, not one part.

qa.q: How might Kamal see his daughter's sketch?
qa.a: With surprise and respect, seeing connections he hadn't put together.

grounding: Shows a teenager understanding how rain, drainage, roots and fertilizer interact on a farm.

passage: In Osaka, Hiroshi, sixteen, was annoyed that the school bus was always late. He and his friend Oskar decided to find out why. They timed the bus for a week and made a chart. It was late on days when the market opened, because delivery trucks blocked the road. It was also late on rainy days, when more parents drove. And since school started at the same time as the office rush, the traffic was worst then. Oskar said, "So it's not the driver." "It's everything together," Hiroshi said. They sent their chart to the school office with a suggestion: start ten minutes later.

qa.q: What blocked the road on market days?
qa.a: Delivery trucks.

qa.q: What might Hiroshi have felt when he saw the pattern in their chart?
qa.a: He probably felt satisfied and a bit surprised, realising the lateness came from many causes.

qa.q: What makes their suggestion to the school sensible?
qa.a: It targets one variable they can change, the start time, within the whole system.

qa.q: How might the bus driver see their findings?
qa.a: Relieved that someone noticed the delays weren't the driver's fault.

grounding: Shows teenagers working out how several separate factors combine to make a bus late.

passage: The school canteen queue was always chaos at lunch. Trisha, fourteen, and Siddharth were on the student council and decided to figure out why. They stood by the counter with a notebook. Two bells rang at the same time, so everyone arrived together. The popular samosas sold out first, so people rushed. Only one cashier was open. "If we change one thing, does it fix it?" Siddharth asked. Trisha tapped her pen against her chin, then drew circles and arrows. "If we stagger the bells, the rush spreads out. Then one cashier is enough." They took the diagram to the principal.

qa.q: How many cashiers were open?
qa.a: Only one cashier was open.

qa.q: What might Trisha have been feeling as she drew the circles and arrows?
qa.a: She seemed curious and absorbed, excited to see how the pieces fit together.

qa.q: Why is staggering the bells a smart first step?
qa.a: It changes the variable that drives the others, the rush, so the rest of the system copes.

qa.q: How might the principal see the students' diagram?
qa.a: With interest, maybe impressed that they looked at the whole system, not just blamed the cashier.

grounding: Shows teenagers mapping how bells, food choices and staff interact to cause a canteen rush.

passage:
Dear Jomon Chettan,
You asked what our school project is. It's the pond behind the Kuttanad school. Last year it was full of fish. This year there's green scum everywhere and hardly any fish. At first I thought someone had poisoned it. But when we tested it, it's more complicated. The farms nearby started using more fertiliser. The rain washes it into the pond. The fertiliser feeds the algae, the algae spreads and blocks the sunlight, the underwater plants die, and without plants there's less oxygen, so the fish die. And fewer fish means the mosquitoes that the fish used to eat are increasing. Everything's connected! Our teacher wants us to suggest one change. I think we should talk to the farmers first.
Your cousin, Farhan

qa.q: What covers the pond this year?
qa.a: Green scum.

qa.q: How does Farhan feel about discovering how everything is connected?
qa.a: Farhan feels excited and amazed by how one change in the fertiliser affects the whole pond.

qa.q: What did Farhan suggest as a first step, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Talking to the farmers first, because the fertiliser from their fields is where the chain starts.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel reading the email?
qa.a: Jomon would likely be interested and impressed by how carefully Farhan traced the problem.

grounding: A teenager writes to a cousin explaining how fertiliser, algae, oxygen, fish and mosquitoes in a pond are linked.

passage: "So, Francis, you asked why the canteen queue is so bad now. I'm Tanvir, and I've been watching it for a whole week, like a detective. Here's the thing. They added a second counter, right? Should've made it faster. But they moved the bell for Class 9 and 10 to the same time, so double the people come at once. Then the second counter only sells samosas, so everyone who wants a sandwich still waits at the first. And because the line's long, people skip the drink stall, so it's empty, and the drink guy got moved to help, which slows the samosas. See? Every fix changed something else. I told the principal, and she wants me to draw it on a chart for the student council. Me! Drawing arrows for the principal."

qa.q: What does the second counter sell?
qa.a: Only samosas.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about being asked to make a chart for the student council?
qa.a: Tanvir feels proud and surprised, amused to be drawing arrows for the principal.

qa.q: What could the school try, based on Tanvir's observations?
qa.a: It could stagger the class bells again or let both counters sell sandwiches, then check how the queue changes.

qa.q: How might the principal see Tanvir's week of watching?
qa.a: She likely sees it as useful, detailed thinking that could help fix the problem.

grounding: A teenager explains to a friend how several changes interact to make the canteen queue worse.

passage: I'm Jagdish, Nandini's uncle. Every morning I drop her at school in Kochi, and we get stuck at the gate. Last month she started noting things in a small book. On rainy days, more parents drove, so more cars. When the school bus came late, parents parked in the bus lane. When the bus couldn't stop, kids got off on the road, and the guards had to stop traffic, making it worse. She drew circles and arrows linking all of it. I thought she was just doodling. Then she showed her diagram to the principal and suggested a drop-off lane with a teacher on rainy days. I watched them talk for a long time. I don't know what she was thinking, but she looked very serious and calm.

qa.q: Where do parents park when the school bus comes late?
qa.a: In the bus lane.

qa.q: What might Nandini have been feeling as she talked to the principal?
qa.a: She was probably confident and determined, looking serious and calm.

qa.q: What was clever about Nandini's suggestion?
qa.a: It targeted a link in the chain, rainy-day drop-offs, instead of just blaming one group.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see Nandini's work?
qa.a: He first thought she was doodling, but is now impressed by how seriously she took it.

grounding: An uncle watches his niece map how weather, buses and parking interact at the school gate.

passage:
Before: In June, Sharmila, fifteen, takes charge of the school garden project. She plants tomatoes and waters them every day. They wilt anyway. She blames the heat.

During, in July: Divyansh, from her group, points out that the soil under the tomatoes stays wet and smelly. They dig and find the drain pipe blocked. Then they notice fewer bees since the gardener sprayed pesticide on the roses nearby. Fewer bees, fewer flowers turning into fruit.

After, in September: They fix the drain, water only in the evenings, and ask the gardener to stop spraying near the vegetables. They plant marigolds to attract bees. The tomatoes start setting fruit.

Sharmila draws a diagram for the class: water, soil, bees, spray, all connected with arrows. "It wasn't one problem," she says. "It was the whole system."

qa.q: What did Sharmila and Divyansh find blocked?
qa.a: They found the drain pipe blocked.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when the tomatoes wilted in June?
qa.a: Sharmila felt frustrated and puzzled, blaming the heat.

qa.q: What did Sharmila learn about solving the garden problem?
qa.a: That many parts, like drainage, watering, bees and pesticide, interact, so she had to fix several things together.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel about his role in the project?
qa.a: Divyansh likely felt proud that his observation about the soil helped uncover the real problem.

grounding: Over a term, a teenager learns how water, soil, bees and pesticide interact as a system in the school garden.

passage:
Keerthana, you asked why I get angry when people waste water. Your Rashmi Paati will tell you.

When I was fourteen, our village well never dried. Then a factory came up nearby and dug deep borewells. At the same time, the forest on the hill was cut for a road.

That summer, our well dried in April. Everyone blamed the rain. But I watched: less forest meant the rain ran off instead of sinking in. The factory pumps drew water from underneath. More people came for factory jobs, so more buckets at the well.

I told my father, "It's not the rain. It's everything together." He didn't believe me at first.

Two years later, the panchayat planted trees and made check dams. It took years, but the well filled again.

So, Keerthana, when you waste water, remember it's all connected.

qa.q: When did the well dry that summer?
qa.a: The well dried in April.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel when her father didn't believe her?
qa.a: Young Rashmi probably felt frustrated but sure of what she had noticed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rashmi's story?
qa.a: When the panchayat planted trees and made check dams, addressing the connected causes, and the well slowly filled again.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's father have seen the well at first?
qa.a: He probably believed the rain was the only cause, like everyone else.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at fourteen, she saw deforestation, borewells and population growth interact to dry the village well.

passage:
The school inspection was on Monday, and the canteen was a mess. Jasleen, sixteen, and Minakshi from the student council had just the weekend to fix the food waste problem.

On Saturday they watched the canteen at lunch. Half the rice was thrown away. Why?

They found several reasons. The portion was fixed, too big for the younger kids. Lunch break was only fifteen minutes, so many didn't finish. And the bins were right by the door, so dumping was easy.

"If we just tell people not to waste, nothing changes," Minakshi said.

So they proposed three things together: two portion sizes, a five-minute longer lunch for the juniors, and moving the bins further in.

On Monday, the inspector asked about waste. Jasleen showed their diagram. "One change alone won't fix it. They're all linked."

qa.q: How long was the lunch break?
qa.a: Lunch break was only fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel showing the diagram to the inspector?
qa.a: Jasleen was probably nervous but confident about their understanding of the problem.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen and Minakshi propose several changes at once?
qa.a: They saw that portion size, lunch time and bin placement all interacted, so one change alone wouldn't fix it.

qa.q: How might the younger students be affected by the changes?
qa.a: They would get smaller portions and more time, so they'd waste less and feel less rushed.

grounding: Under time pressure, two teenagers see how portion size, time and bin placement interact to cause canteen waste.

passage: The water tank in their Bengaluru apartment block ran dry for the third time that week, and the residents' chat group was full of angry messages blaming the watchman. Gargi sat on the stairs with a notebook and her friend Kashish. "It's not one thing," Gargi said, drawing arrows. "Two new blocks moved in, so more people. The borewell level's down after the weak monsoon. Everyone runs their motors at six a.m., so the pressure drops. And the tanker comes at noon, when half the tank's already gone." Kashish stared. "So if we staggered motor times..." "And moved the tanker to morning, yes, it might hold." Gargi posted the diagram to the group. The angry messages slowed.

qa.q: Who was the chat group blaming?
qa.a: They were blaming the watchman.

qa.q: Why did Gargi sit down to draw arrows instead of joining the angry messages?
qa.a: She felt curious and calm enough to look for causes, and seemed uneasy that one person was being blamed.

qa.q: What could the residents try based on Gargi's diagram?
qa.a: They could stagger motor times and ask for the tanker in the morning, then watch whether the tank holds.

qa.q: What would change for the watchman if residents understood Gargi's diagram?
qa.a: The watchman would likely stop being blamed unfairly, since the shortage comes from several causes working together.

grounding: Shows a teenager tracing how several separate causes combine to empty a building's water tank.
